1:
Nobody places the psalm confidently. Clarke says outright that it contains no notes of time or place and no certain evidence of its author; it may be David's under Saul's persecution, though some assign it to Jeremiah, one verse opening with exactly the words of a verse in that prophet. Delitzsch enlarges the case — several passages answer to Jeremiah and Lamentations, and the psalm's plaintive tenderness recalls him — but refuses to let resemblance settle it: Jeremiah's speech is so steeped in the Psalter that the parallel may as easily be his reminiscence as this psalm's borrowing. Calvin reports a conjecture placing it after David's escape from the wilderness of Maon, and calls it doubtful while allowing it. Augustine reads the title instead: the word added there signifies a transport of mind produced by panic or revelation, and this psalm shows chiefly the panic of God's people under persecution. He then divides the speakers — the Mediator first, the redeemed people giving thanks next, the prophet interposed twice at the close.

The opening profession is the psalm's foundation, not its ornament. Gill insists on the tense — not I have trusted, nor I will trust, but I do, a continued act, and directed to no creature. Calvin sees the same continuance and observes that nothing but faith is brought forward, deliverance promised only because safety depends on God's power; hope that depends on God cannot be disappointed. Spurgeon calls it the sheet anchor cast out in the storm, put first lest trial drive it from mind; no merit is mentioned, and it would dishonour God if faith went unrewarded. Calvin finds the next clause capable of two constructions: though deprived of thy help now, cast me not off for ever, distress for a time set against lasting confusion; or, whatever befalls, be ready to stretch out thy hand as the case requires. Ellicott gives the literal form: let me not for ever be ashamed.

Henry pairs the petitions with a doctrine: faith and prayer go together, for he that believes should pray and he that prays believe. God is asked to deliver not in mercy only but in righteousness, as a judge between the psalmist and his persecutors; to deliver speedily, lest deferred rescue exhaust the faith that waits; and, failing that, to shelter within the trouble — a fastness framed by nature, a house of defence framed by art. The prayer for guidance governs conscience and prudence at once: nothing unlawful, nothing unwise. Clarke makes the stooping ear concrete: put thy ear to my lips, as with the dying. Ellicott prefers my cliff fortress where the noun changes, and puts the verbs in the future: thou wilt lead and guide, thou wilt pull me out. To the charge that praying for protection and then asserting confidence is illogical he grants it: this is the logic of the heart, and of every prayer of faith.

The fifth verse carries the psalm's most famous words, and the readers divide over their first sense. Gill takes them of life entrusted to a faithful Creator, of the soul and its eternal safety, or of a man expecting death and committing a spirit that outlives the body. Clarke traces the Latin form's long service among the dying, said by the sick while they could speak and by the priest when they could not, and kept in Latin inside English prayers as though the tongue were sovereign. Christ, he notes, omitted its second half as unsuited to himself though suited to the redeemed. Wesley keeps it practical: the spirit is committed for preservation, on the strength of past rescue. Ellicott dissents from all of this. The words have upheld a long line of Christian worthies at the end, but death was not in the psalmist's thought: it was in life, amid trouble, that he deposited his spirit with God as a trust.
6:
The vanities hated in the sixth verse are read narrowly by most, broadly by one. Ellicott gives the literal breath of lies and calls them undoubtedly idols; Clarke agrees, an idol being nothing in the world, much promised and nothing given; Wesley allows either idols or the curious arts and every sort of divination. Gill takes the whole field: divination, all will-worship, which being unauthorised is worship in vain, errors and heresies, and finally all worldly enjoyment as vanity and vexation of spirit. The turn to thanksgiving draws Spurgeon's best writing. In our most importunate intercessions we must find breathing time to bless the Lord, since praise never hinders prayer but refreshes it — delightful to hear the cymbals when the dolorous sackbut rules the hour. To be known in adversity, he adds, is to be owned by one who thinks no worse of his friends for their rags.

Clarke turns the same clause into a maxim. Where a friend so called finds it convenient not to know his friend in poverty, God acknowledged him as his own when all had forsaken him. Human friendships fail; the Friend of sinners does not. Ellicott finds the next phrase to be the exact wording David used in consulting the oracle by the ephod, then refuses to argue authorship from it, the phrase being common. Henry marks the change of plea in the darkest stretch: having appealed to God's righteousness, the psalmist now appeals to his mercy, the argument being simply the greatness of his misery. He reads the ruined health as evidence against temperament — a man ruddy and sanguine, with a genius for music and a record of daring, who has nonetheless wept out his eyes. Let the airy and gay take heed of extremes: God can make them melancholy if they will not otherwise learn to be serious.

The physical detail is taken seriously. Clarke lists what grief does — spoils digestion, impairs the nerves, hastens death — and notes that the bowels are named as the tender part and the seat of compassion. He then calls the Hebrew word for sighing a natural sound rather than a coined word, the noise a distressed mind makes, near enough the same in every language; the Irish cry, he says, is precisely the same sound and sense. Ellicott reports the old belief that an eye could weep itself away, and prefers body to belly, since mind and body suffered together. Spurgeon compresses it: misery moves mercy, no further reasoning needed, and tears draw their salt from our strength.

Over one clause the readers split. Henry takes the failing strength as owned desert: against Saul the psalmist could insist on his righteousness, but as an affliction laid on him by God he confesses he deserved it. Ellicott and Wesley read the word as the suffering that follows sin rather than the sin itself, and note that the Greek and Latin render it poverty. On the reproach, Clarke reconstructs the social ruin: proscribed at court, thought dangerous by neighbours, avoided by those who knew him best, shunned as though contagious. Wesley adds that they kept away to prevent their own danger. Ellicott finds the adverb rendered especially out of place and would make it a noun meaning burden, with the watchers fluttering away like frightened birds. Gill notes that reproach is as it is made: under divine support the saints count it great riches, at other times it seizes their spirits and breaks their hearts. He allows that being forgotten as a dead man may mean forgotten by God, and calls that the weakness of the psalmist's faith, not the truth of his case. Ellicott closes by unsettling the most quoted phrase: the noun probably means conspiracy rather than terror, and the slander is a whisper, so what he heard was the many whispering conspiracy all around — a pretended panic covering a plot.
14:
The turn is marked by a pronoun. Ellicott calls it emphatic, set against the pretended panic and the real dangers alike. Delitzsch draws it out: though an offscouring of all people, and though God appears to have given him up in anger, the psalmist confides in him even so, with the prayer of appropriating faith. Spurgeon notices that the section renews the earlier petitions, as earnest wrestlers try the same hold again and again; faith is the shield, and while it holds the battle may go hard but its issue is settled. He was no fair-weather believer, but kept his faith in a sharp frost and wrapped it about him as a garment; the adhesion is offered to God as a reason to hurry. Gill sees faith reviving under discouraging views; Clarke reads the confession as a settlement: thou hast been my helper hitherto, and I have taken thee for my portion.

The next clause is the psalm's most quoted after the fifth verse. Gill takes it against the enemies directly: the time of his life and death was fixed by God, and no enemy could take it before then; prosperity and adversity alike are at God's disposal, which is a quieting thought. Ellicott widens it to the vicissitudes of human life, which the Greek and Latin render destinies, so that no machination can prevail against one whom God means to deliver; and he sets its security against another Hebrew idiom, in which a man's soul is continually in his own hand. Spurgeon makes it pastoral: we are not waifs upon the ocean of fate but steered by wisdom towards a desired haven, and providence is a soft pillow for anxious heads, an anodyne for care, a grave for despair.

The petitions that follow go quickly. Ellicott hears the priestly blessing echoed in the request for a shining face; Clarke asks only to know that God is reconciled, after which all must be well, and renders the next plea literally as save me in thy mercy. On the lying lips Ellicott notes a different word from the previous verse, so the sense is to be made dumb, and prefers arrogant to grievous, the phrase running literally in pride and contempt. Gill guesses at the courtiers who told Saul that David sought his throne, while Clarke asks only that their pride be abated and their devices confounded.

The last verse opens into praise, and its two verbs divide them. Henry takes them as two kinds of goodness: one laid up, an inheritance reserved, and one wrought here — enough in bank and enough in hand, promised to all who fear God and performed for those who trust him, taking hold of the promise by faith and putting it in suit. If what is laid up is not wrought for us, he says, the fault is our own, because we do not believe. Those whom men load with slanders, he adds, God loads with benefits, and the goodness rolls away their reproach. Spurgeon makes the same division and furnishes it — the caskets of the promises, the granaries of providence — but pauses first over the exclamation, singular in the middle of so much sorrow. The psalmist does not say how great it is because he could not: holy amazement uses interjections where adjectives fail, and if we cannot measure we can marvel. Ellicott declines the two-part reading and takes the first verb as hidden, a treasure now brought out before the sons of men — also Wesley's sense of a favour not always manifested but drawn out when needed. Clarke attaches the closing phrase to the trusting rather than the display, making it the boldness of those who confess God openly amid a crooked generation; and the store is infinite — enough for all, for each, for evermore, laid up where neither devils nor men can reach it.
20:
The hiding place is described three ways. Clarke renders it with the covering of thy countenance and makes the concealment total: a life so hidden that enemies cannot find it, a refuge Satan dare not approach; the pavilion is the innermost part of the tent, implying communion as well as shelter. Ellicott prefers the hiding-place of thy countenance, one of several such images in the Psalms. Wesley offers three readings without choosing: a presence chamber where God's eye and hand gird them; the tabernacle, which none might enter save the high priest; or a secret favour saving by unknown methods. Henry names the danger: pride would trample them down and contentious men pick quarrels, and where tongues are at strife the good get the worst — pride endangering liberty, perverse disputing endangering truth.

Ellicott will not leave the first of those words alone: the parallelism and the Greek favour rough or wrangling talk rather than arrogance, and one lexicographer renders it conspiracies — making the verse a rescue from slander rather than insolence. The thanksgiving raises a plainer question: what strong city? Clarke argues for Ziklag, the fortified town given David by the king of Gath, and rejects Keilah, where he had only warning of a treacherous design and found the walls no refuge; but he allows the phrase may mean simply that under God's protection he was as safe as if walled in. Wesley says Keilah without hesitation. Henry keeps both, recalling that God preserved him in caves and woods as safely as in any city, and that at Keilah the mercy was double — he rescued the inhabitants, then was rescued from them when they would have handed him over. Ellicott declines all of it, taking the phrase as a general image of divine protection, and reads the verb as making the kindness manifest rather than showing it.

Over the confession, they divide between the feet and the mind. Gill takes the haste as literal flight from Saul, and Ellicott agrees — in my fleeing away in fear — though several ancient translators give in my confusion. Wesley, Clarke and Henry take it inwardly: passion displaced consideration and weakened faith, and the psalmist concluded from the number of his enemies that he must fall. Henry treats the sentence as recorded against himself: though he had express promises and long experience of God's care, he entertained a jealous thought and told it to God's face; and what is spoken amiss in haste must be repented of at leisure, particularly what is spoken distrustfully of God. His faith failed, Henry observes; the promise did not.

The closing exhortation is Spurgeon's and Clarke's best. Spurgeon calls it affecting because it is love towards a smiting God: to bless him who gives is easy, but to cling to him who takes is a work of grace. If the saints do not love the Lord, he asks, who will? Love is the universal debt of the saved family, and reasons are given, since believing love is not blind. On courage he is brisk — let no craven thoughts blanch your cheek, for fear weakens and courage strengthens, and the promised strengthening puts power into the fountain of vitality. Clarke restricts the command to those who can obey it, only the saints partaking of the divine nature, and defines the faithful as those who bring forth the fruits of love, to whom duty is delight. Against these he sets the proud doer, and cannot contain himself: a sinner, a fallen spirit, an heir of wretchedness, and proud — proud of what? Such men shall get their due, their whole due, nothing but their due. Ellicott adds a quiet correction: preserving the faithful may be better rendered as keeping faith. Gill ends where the psalm does: the distressed may take heart, their case being no worse than the psalmist's, and he was delivered.
